As the gaming industry continues to grow, so does the demand for high-quality requirements engineering practices. Our work provides an initial framework for requirements elicitation in gaming, offering a valuable resource for future research. Potential areas of exploration include applying our framework to other game genres, incorporating user feedback, and developing evaluation metrics for gaming requirements.

The task of optimizing hyperparameters for a model that trains on a private dataset through multiple iterations is complicated, as it cannot be achieved through traditional methods like grid search. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a Bayesian optimization framework, specifically a Bayesian model that learns the relationship between hyperparameters and the model's performance. This approach allows us to utilize black-box oracles that evaluate the model's performance, and we explore two distinct approaches to doing so: one that involves training a separate model for each grid point, and another that involves training a single model and using it to estimate the performance of different hyperparameter settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on real-world data, and show that it can outperform traditional methods like grid search.

In 1984, Davis introduced the concept of groupoids of cycles, which involves constructing a geometric structure, denoted as $\mathcal{D}(G)$, from a given group $G$ and its generating set $S$. This construction results in a collection of spheres, with the number of spheres corresponding to the size of the generating set $S$. In this study, we modify Davis's construction by replacing the spheres with Coxeter groups, thereby creating a geometric structure associated with any group $G$ and its generating set $S$, which consists of spaces related to the elements of $S$. This new structure, denoted as $\mathcal{D}(G,S)$, is constructed as an $S$-fold CW-complex, with each $n$-cell corresponding to an element of the cosets $S\times S\times \cdots \times S$ of length $n$. We demonstrate that the fundamental group of $\mathcal{D}(G,S)$ is isomorphic to $G$, and the link of each $n$-cell is the Cayley graph of the Coxeter group associated with the element in the coset.

This paper presents an updated version of the Notox Python package, a tool for estimating noise correlations in detectors and estimating their impact on the accuracy of measurements. The new version, 0.4.0, features significant improvements in functionality, including the ability to handle time-varying noise correlations, a user-friendly interface for creating noise models, and the ability to estimate the bias and variance of measurements for arbitrary data and source models. The new version of Notox is demonstrated using real LIGO detector data, showing that the improved functionality can significantly improve the accuracy of measurements, particularly in cases where the noise correlations are complex and time-varying. The new version of Notox is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0 and is available on GitHub.

This study focuses on the detailed chemical composition of 10 stars from the APOGEE-2 dataset, which are characterized by their unusual abundances. A thorough analysis of residual patterns across various chemical elements is conducted, revealing the chemically distinctive nature of these stars. By comparing their chemical compositions to those of other APOGEE-2 datasets, we found that these stars share similar ages, metallicities, and rotational velocities, yet exhibit unique chemical signatures. The discrepancies in residual patterns between the stars and the datasets are primarily attributed to variations in $\alpha$-element and iron group element ratios, as well as the presence of rare elements. The analysis of these elements provides insights into the formation and evolution of stellar populations, and the results suggest that these stars may have originated from the same birth cluster. The study also highlights the importance of APOGEE-2 data in the identification of chemically distinctive stars and the potential for further research into the formation and evolution of stellar populations.

This study proposes a novel approach to accurately forecast the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors within a Twitter network. We discovered that certain precursor indicators, such as the presence of specific locations and the frequency of certain keywords, can significantly influence the spread of rumors. By leveraging a unique feature extraction method and a novel regression model, we successfully achieved a notable improvement in prediction accuracy, resulting in a 10% reduction in the root mean square error compared to previous methods.

We have utilized a sample of 1118 nearby Fornax cluster planetary nebulae, identified in the g,r,i,z bands by the DESI Legacy Survey, to investigate the Fornax cluster's structure and dynamics. By analyzing the PNLF distance modulus distribution, we determined the cluster's average distance to be 25.734±0.016 magnitudes, corresponding to 17.44±0.09 Mpc. Our findings suggest that the PNLF method is a reliable tool for measuring the distances of nearby clusters. Additionally, we derived the line of sight velocity for the cluster, finding it to be 409.8±1.1 km/s, in good agreement with previous studies. By dividing the cluster into 10 radial bins, we were able to map the distance and velocity variations across the cluster, which can be utilized to study the mass distribution and Fornax's dynamics. Our results also suggest that the PNLF method is capable of measuring distance variations within nearby clusters.

We introduce LifeStream, a novel system that automates the creation of high-performance stream aggregations for real-world datasets. LifeStream utilizes machine learning to generate optimized code that can be seamlessly integrated into existing C/C++ applications. By leveraging stream aggregation templates, LifeStream's generated code is easily adaptable to various applications. Our extensive testing on 110 real-world datasets from diverse domains demonstrates that LifeStream's performance rivals top numerical libraries and outperforms HandStream, a state-of-the-art hand-optimized approach, in several cases. LifeStream's stream aggregations are also highly efficient, with minimal memory overhead and excellent cache performance.

This research extends the concept of Bertrand curves to higher dimensions, initially introduced for curves in R^3 and R^4. Specifically, it defines a Bertrand curve for a curve in R^n as one that possesses a Bertrand partner within the same dimension. Notably, it's demonstrated that a Bertrand curve in R^n is uniquely characterized in the space of curves C^{n-1}(R^n), but this definition no longer holds for curves in higher-dimensional spaces. This study also delves into the properties of Bertrand curves in dimensions four and above, exploring their parametric representations and providing specific examples.

In deep learning, researchers often experiment with various loss functions to improve model performance. However, there's a prevailing tendency to stick with commonly used options, neglecting under-represented alternatives. In this research, we investigate the impact of under-explored loss functions on model performance, specifically focusing on KL Divergence, which has been overlooked in recent years. We introduce a novel framework called LossFunctionBench, which provides a comprehensive evaluation of loss functions across multiple tasks and model architectures. Our findings reveal that the choice of loss function can have a significant impact on performance, with a performance variance of up to 10% across different options. We also observe that KL Divergence can yield substantial improvements of up to 15% in certain scenarios, particularly in tasks involving discrete outputs. To facilitate further research, we make our framework and associated data publicly available.

This study investigates the impact of a temperature-controlled boundary on a fluid flow within a two-dimensional square domain, governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. We demonstrate that a sufficiently steep angle of the feedback mechanism, which adjusts the boundary based on flow velocity, can stabilize a stationary solution. Conversely, a steeper angle of the opposite sign induces instability, resulting in the development of a flow with a recirculation pattern. These findings hold true for both scenarios where the domain's boundaries are fixed or subject to different boundary conditions.

A comprehensive theory of strain-induced crystallization in polymers is presented,
drawing on thermodynamic and statistical mechanics principles. This framework
incorporates both glassy and rubbery states of the polymer and is applied to model
its thermomechanical behavior under various mechanical stimuli. The resulting
equations are solved numerically to predict the material's response to different
mechanical stimuli, including monotonic and cyclic loading.

We investigate the interplay between superconductivity and the nodal structure of a Fermi surface in a model featuring two bands and an s-wave pairing mechanism. Our analysis reveals that the topology of the Fermi surface significantly influences the behavior of the magnetic susceptibility within the superconducting state. Specifically, we find that when the nesting condition is met, the susceptibility diverges as the superconducting gap shrinks, whereas in non-neutral configurations, the susceptibility remains finite. These findings are supported by numerical calculations and provide valuable insights into the relationship between superconductivity and Fermi surface topology.

A significant challenge in deploying machine learning systems is providing human feedback in a timely and efficient manner. A promising solution is to have a teacher guide the learning process by offering corrective feedback. However, this approach becomes difficult when the learning system operates in a vast array of situations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework that allows the teacher to offer feedback in a more manageable way. This framework enables the learning system to apply a teacher's guidance in a wide range of scenarios, even when the teacher has limited experience. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in a real-world application involving a machine learning system that predicts the outcomes of soccer matches. This system is designed to handle a wide range of situations, from different teams to different times of the year. We show that our framework can effectively apply the teacher's feedback in this system, even when the teacher has limited experience.

A novel detection technique for CPM signals is proposed, which leverages a maximum likelihood sequence estimator and a trellis diagram to achieve optimal performance. This new method, which utilizes a differential detector, can be seen as a form of differential detection that builds upon conventional approaches. By comparing the error rates of the proposed technique to conventional differential detection, it is shown that the new method can outperform the latter, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratios. Additionally, a form of differential detection is proposed that can be implemented with a differential detector and a maximum likelihood sequence estimator, which can be seen as a way to combine the benefits of both approaches. This new form of differential detection can be seen as a way to achieve a balance between the error rate performance of the proposed technique and the implementation complexity of a maximum likelihood sequence estimator. By comparing the error rates of the proposed technique to differential detection, it is shown that the new form can achieve a balance between the two approaches.

The likelihood of a neutron star and black hole merger producing a detectable electromagnetic signal depends on the distance between the black hole's center and the remaining neutron star after they collide. This distance can vary greatly due to the spinning of the black hole. We've developed a new method to figure out how the size of the neutron star affects the chances of producing such a signal. By using this method, we've determined that the size of the neutron star has a significant impact on the chances of producing an electromagnetic counterpart. Specifically, if the neutron star is smaller, the chances of producing such a signal increase significantly. This has important implications for using gravitational waves to learn more about the neutron star and black hole merger process. We've also found that the size of the neutron star can be estimated by analyzing the spinning of the black hole, which can be done using a specific type of gravitational wave signal.

The accuracy of grand canonical ensemble approximations for closed systems under constant pressure is limited by the system's compressibility, as demonstrated in this study. Specifically, the approximation's error is proportional to the product of the system's compressibility and the relative volume fluctuations in the canonical ensemble, divided by Boltzmann's constant and temperature. This relationship is further expressed in terms of the system's isothermal bulk modulus and the variance of the canonical volume fluctuations. Notably, this error is most pronounced in systems with low volume moduli, such as gaseous systems. Consequently, the condition for the closed system's grand canonical partition function to converge to the square of the grand canonical volume average in the canonical ensemble is that the system's volume moduli must be significantly larger than the product of the system's elastic energy and the square of the canonical volume fluctuations divided by Boltzmann's constant and temperature. This condition is most easily met in systems with low volume moduli, such as gaseous systems.

In this research, we tackle the inconsistency issue in rain generation and removal models, which are typically trained and evaluated in isolation. To address this problem, we propose a new framework that creates a rain generation and removal cycle, allowing us to evaluate the quality of synthetic rain images. Within this framework, we develop two key components: a rain generator and a rain remover. The generator's task is to create realistic rain images from clear input images, while the remover's goal is to restore the original clear image from a rain-generated version. We train these components in a cycle-consistent manner, ensuring that the remover can accurately restore the original clear image from the generated rain image. To further enhance the quality of synthetic rain images, we incorporate a perceptual loss function. We also design a novel evaluation metric, rain-to-clear FID, to assess the realism of the generated rain images. Our framework outperforms existing methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. We make our framework publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhu1997/CRCR.

Human reward signals are frequently obtained through pairwise comparisons, which are more cost-effective and less cognitively demanding than direct ratings. By comparing multiple alternatives in batches, we can enhance the quality of feedback and accelerate the learning process. To leverage this benefit, we propose an algorithm that identifies pairs within batches for comparison, prioritizing pairs with the most uncertain reward values. Our method is evaluated using both simulated data and real human feedback from the Arena-RL environment. The results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms random pair selection, achieving comparable performance to direct ratings while requiring fewer human feedbacks.

The standardization of a logical language's formulation impacts the properties of the corresponding theory of that language. This effect is particularly evident in first-order logic, where the axiomatization of set theory's axioms influences the concept of model companionship. To illustrate this, we examine the relationship between model companionship and the specific axioms used to define set theory. We focus on the Tarski-Godel and von Neumann-Bernays-Godel systems, analyzing the connection between their respective model companionships.

The widespread use of psychoactive drugs poses a significant public health issue, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of consumption patterns. This study leverages the Google Trends API to analyze the search frequencies of 15 psychoactive drugs in the United States from 2004 to 2019. The findings reveal that the search frequencies of these drugs exhibit a fractal pattern, characterized by self-similarity across different time scales. Furthermore, the study identifies a strong correlation between the consumption of certain drugs, with cannabis, cocaine, and heroin displaying particularly high correlation levels. The research also uncovers a notable relationship between the consumption of certain drugs and economic indicators, with the consumption of cannabis, cocaine, and LSD being positively correlated with the unemployment rate. The study's findings have implications for the development of early warning systems for drug consumption patterns and the design of public health policies.

The HHL algorithm, a quantum linear solver, is widely used as a subroutine in many other quantum algorithms. However, the NISQ-HHL algorithm, a real-time HHL implementation, is not well-documented. In this research, we propose a novel approach to implement the HHL algorithm on NISQ devices and present a concrete example of its application. Our method incorporates a new inverting technique and a new state preparation method, and our results show that our approach can achieve a comparable outcome to the previous NISQ-HHL algorithm with fewer resources.

This paper introduces a novel technique, bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM), which is incorporated into the automated speech recognition system. The integration of BiAM allows for a more effective connection between speech representations and pre-trained language information. The attention mechanism is utilized to seamlessly blend the speech representations with the linguistic information in both forward and reverse directions. The proposed method is applied within the context of transducer-based speech recognition systems. The results obtained from the proposed technique demonstrate a significant improvement in the system's performance, achieving a 0.15 character error rate reduction in the Chinese speech recognition task.

We investigate the behavior of stationary configurations for the fractional Ginzburg-Landau functional in both two-dimensional and one-dimensional settings, focusing on the minimal energy threshold as the parameter s approaches one.

We investigate the phase diagram of a superconducting nanowire with a fixed amount of dissipation, where we find that the nanowire exhibits a critical voltage threshold beyond which its resistance increases from zero to that of normal state. We find that this critical voltage can be adjusted by the applied voltage, and we find that the critical voltage can be adjusted by the applied voltage, and we find that the critical voltage can be adjusted by the applied voltage.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, a brown dwarf, by comparing it to similar objects such as 51 Peg b, HD 209458 b, and HD 149026 b. By examining the atmospheric conditions of these intermediate-sized objects, we can gain a better understanding of their formation processes. Our study utilized a detailed model to fit the observed spectrum of GJ 229b in the infrared range, which enabled us to estimate its temperature, pressure, and chemical composition. Our results indicate that GJ 229b has a temperature of approximately 650 K, a pressure of around 1 bar, and a chemical composition that is similar to that of a solar mixture. Our study also revealed the presence of water vapor and carbon monoxide in the atmosphere of GJ 229b, which are important indicators of its formation history. Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge about the atmospheres of exoplanets and brown dwarfs, and they have important implications for the development of new techniques for detecting and characterizing these objects.

To address the challenge of predicting videos from unseen angles, our approach leverages a neural network to generate a single, two-dimensional feature that not only allows for the reconstruction of videos from various angles but also facilitates accurate predictions from new angles. This capability is achieved by employing a dual network structure, which is trained to minimize discrepancies between the reconstructed and original videos, as well as between the outputs of the dual network and the original input. The use of this dual representation enables our approach to achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, which typically rely on single network structures.

We propose a novel approach to photonic beam splitting using higher-order modes,
which allows for precise control over output intensity ratios. By employing a
device that couples distinct mode pairs, we can create a beam splitter capable of
manipulating both amplitude and phase differences between the output modes. This
approach offers a potential solution for enhancing the performance of photonic
quantum logic gates. We demonstrate the feasibility of our design using silicon
photonic waveguides and show that it can operate effectively at a wavelength of
$1.55\mu m$.

Using the heavy quark effective theory and light cone sum rules, we've derived resonance mass spectra for various baryon states within the infinite momentum frame. These calculations employ two distinct approaches to determine mass spectra for different combinations of light quark states and heavy quarks. The results from both methods are found to be in close agreement, and the mass spectra for the $B_c$ meson are also derived and compared with existing experimental data.

A mathematical model has been developed to simulate the spread of airborne pathogens, specifically focusing on the behavior of aerosols in a confined space. The model takes into account the emission of aerosols by an infected individual, their dispersion, and eventual settling. The model's performance was evaluated against a more complex computational fluid dynamics model, and the results showed that the well-mixed model can accurately predict the concentration of aerosols around an infected person. The simplicity of the well-mixed model makes it a practical tool for designing infection control strategies. The model's limitations were also discussed, and potential areas for future research were identified.

Quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence effects are influenced by the direction of x-ray photon propagation in relation to a nanophotonic structure. When x-ray photons travel parallel to a waveguide, the Casimir pressure causes a transverse shift of the beam, whereas perpendicular propagation results in a longitudinal shift. Additionally, the Casimir force induces a phase shift that depends on the direction of propagation, with the effect being more pronounced when x-ray photons travel perpendicular to the waveguide.

We have developed an algorithm that produces fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space, related to a specific family known as the Brieskorn varieties, extending to higher dimensions at odd numbers. The algorithm utilizes a specific family of vector fields to iteratively refine polyhedra constructed from complex equations, ultimately yielding three-dimensional polyhedra with desirable properties.

By employing a unique coding technique, we aim to detect any unauthorized modifications made during transmission. Researchers have extensively studied the properties of twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ through first-principles calculations, but a more accurate understanding requires considering lattice relaxations and electron interactions. To address this, we performed a comprehensive analysis of plasmon energies and behaviors in TBLMoS$_2$ by utilizing the random phase approximation, lattice relaxations, and doping effects. Our results indicate that lattice relaxations significantly impact plasmon energies and behaviors, with longitudinal plasmons in the energy range of 1-3 eV being particularly sensitive to these changes. Additionally, we found that doping has a minimal effect on plasmon energies and behaviors, with the plasma frequency being primarily determined by the number of electrons. Our analysis also reveals that plasmon dispersion is highly sensitive to doping levels, with the dispersion becoming flatter at higher doping levels. Furthermore, we found that plasmon modes in TBLMoS$_2$ are highly localized, with the localization length being primarily determined by the screening of the lattice. Our results provide valuable insights into the electronic properties of TBLMoS$_2$ and have implications for the development of novel 2D materials.

This paper investigates almost conformal Ricci solitons on a manifold M and establishes several key properties. Firstly, we derive an integral formula for these solitons. Secondly, we identify conditions under which an almost conformal Ricci soliton becomes an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton, specifically when the soliton function's gradient is not zero. Additionally, we determine that the transformation function must be constant if the soliton transformation function is not zero. Finally, we examine almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons with a non-zero transformation and prove that they cannot be shrinking. We also provide examples of such solitons.

Magnetospheres are created by the interaction between magnetic fields and stellar winds, and they can be found in both stars and planets. The study of magnetospheres is essential for comprehending the behavior of stellar winds and the magnetic fields of planets. The research paper discusses the magnetospheres of stars and planets, highlighting their similarities and differences. It also highlights the challenges in studying planetary magnetospheres and the potential for future research. The paper provides an overview of the current knowledge on stellar and planetary magnetospheres, and it identifies potential areas for future investigation.

We have created Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers and measured their transport properties, revealing that the sample's conductivity and Hall effect are primarily influenced by the Bismuth layers. The conductivity and Hall coefficient can be adjusted by varying the thickness of the Bismuth layers. The samples exhibit a scattering mechanism that is a combination of the Mattheissen's rule and the parallel conductance model. The samples' magnetoresistance is positive and reaches a maximum of 10% at a magnetic field of 1 Tesla, perpendicular to the sample's surface.

This study investigates the existence of positive solutions for N-dimensional Schrödinger equations with a fractional potential, where we prove that at least one positive solution exists under specific conditions.

When training a neural network, we can impose a bounded Lipschitz constant on the network's transformation to prevent overfitting. This approach is a form of regularization that is particularly effective when the training data is noisy. In this paper, we investigate the impact of different $p$-norms on the input data when using this regularization approach. We provide theoretical results that show the relationship between the choice of $p$-norm and the regularization's performance. We also conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the impact of different $p$-norms on the neural network's generalization ability. Our results indicate that the choice of $p$-norm can have a significant impact on the network's performance, and that the $l_1$-norm can be particularly effective in certain scenarios.

Human language is inherently sequential, which poses a challenge for our comprehension of its underlying hierarchical nature. To address this, we investigate the extent to which sequential models can learn the syntactic structure of sentences without explicit guidance. We evaluate the capacity of these models to capture the hierarchical organization of sentences by analyzing their implicit representations of syntactic trees. We find that various sequential models, including LSTMs and Transformers, can indeed represent the hierarchical structure of sentences, albeit with some limitations. We further investigate the extent to which these models can utilize the syntactic tree to predict the next word in a sentence. We find that the LSTMs can effectively utilize the tree to make these predictions, while the Transformers struggle to do so. We also examine the extent to which these models can capture the syntactic dependencies between words in a sentence. We find that the LSTMs can represent the local dependencies well, while their global representations are limited. We also investigate the extent to which these models can capture the syntactic categories of words in a sentence. We find that the LSTMs can capture the local categories well, while their global representations are limited. A unique exoplanet, HD80606b, experiences a significant temperature fluctuation due to its highly elliptical orbit, which causes its surface temperature to vary from 1,300 K to 2,100 K. This temperature change is accompanied by a corresponding shift in the planet's spectral characteristics. To accurately determine the planet's effective temperature, we analyzed the observed spectra of HD 80606b b in the 1.2-2.4 $\mu$m range, which were obtained from the Keck II telescope using the NIRSPEC instrument. By comparing the observed spectra to synthetic spectra, we found that the planet's effective temperature changes from 1,850 K to 2,200 K as it moves from periastron to apastron. This temperature range is consistent with the previously reported values.

The rise of wearable technology has facilitated the creation of personalized exercise programs that can be customized to an individual's physical condition and rehabilitation needs. To encourage adherence to these programs, gamification techniques have been employed, incorporating game elements into the training process. However, the use of gamification can also lead to excessive focus on the game, potentially neglecting the intended physical activity. To address this issue, we propose a framework that utilizes machine learning to determine the optimal level of gamification for a given user. This framework is designed to balance the user's rehabilitation and engagement needs by analyzing their behavior and adjusting the program's difficulty and feedback accordingly. The proposed approach is validated through a series of experiments, which demonstrate its ability to achieve this balance and improve the user's progress towards their health goals.

This study establishes the equivalence of $Γ-$convergence for geometrically nonlinear elasticity and linearised elasticity to brittle fracture energies, specifically the $Γ-$convergence of the functional $\int_{\Omega} W(\nabla u) dx$ to that of crack surface area, under the condition of bounded strain, where $W$ is a frame invariant, piecewise quadratic elasticity function. The results hold true for both linearised elasticity and geometrically nonlinear elasticity, where the latter uses the full nonlinear elasticity function. The proof relies on the construction of piecewise affine functions, and the use of a specific type of nonconvex elasticity function allows for a more straightforward proof compared to previous studies. The approach used here can also be applied to other types of elasticity functions, such as those with higher degree growth, and the results hold true in any dimension greater than one.

The LHC's vector leptoquark searches have been conducted, focusing on first- and second-generation fermions. Initial investigations were carried out for color-triplet vector leptoquarks in the approximation of the heavy mass limit, where pairs of fermions can be treated as an effective interaction with a leptoquark. To enhance the precision of signal modeling beyond this approximation, a Next-to-Leading Order plus Parton Shower (NLO+PS) approach was employed, utilizing the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO framework. This approach was applied to top-squark and vector leptoquark searches, with top-squark results being presented here for the first time. These analyses were performed at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, with various decay modes and mass ranges considered, with some results being novel. The analysis was also extended to top squark coannihilation scenarios, with constraints derived from LHC searches and dark matter relic density.

This study introduces a novel Deep Neural Network (DNN) framework for enhancing the quality of low-dose Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images. The proposed method leverages prior knowledge from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data to improve the performance of low-dose PET images. The framework consists of two primary components: a low-dose PET to MRI-guided PET image translation network and a low-dose PET to MRI-guided PET image refinement network. The translation network learns the mapping between MRI and PET images, while the refinement network learns the mapping between low-dose PET and MRI-guided PET images. The framework is trained in an end-to-end manner using a supervised learning approach. The proposed DNN framework is evaluated on both synthetic and real low-dose PET images, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates the effectiveness of neural coreference resolution models when incorporating contextual information, specifically in relation to the theory of linguistic centering. We analyzed the impact of contextualized word representations, such as BERT, on coreference prediction and found that these models can both reinforce and contradict the predictions of the neural models and centering theory. Our findings suggest that the choice of contextualization method can significantly influence the performance of the models, and that further research is needed to understand the relationship between contextualized embeddings, coreference resolution, and centering theory.

We introduce a novel graph parameter, known as treewidth, applicable to directed graphs and demonstrate that it can effectively complement existing graph parameters in facilitating directed acyclic graph (DAG) parameterization. Our research reveals that the treewidth of a directed graph is inherently bounded by its undirected counterpart's treewidth. Moreover, we develop a polynomial-time reduction from any directed graph to its undirected counterpart, ensuring that the corresponding width values remain equivalent. This discovery has significant implications for combining treewidth with other graph parameters, such as pathwidth, which can be expressed in terms of undirected width values. Our findings also suggest that certain parameterized problems, including the Longest Path problem, can be solved using algorithms with running times of $f(\text{tw}+ \text{sp})n^{O(1)}$ on graphs where sp represents the sum of treewidth and pathwidth.

Using optimization to find the best system settings offers several advantages.
First, it provides a clear path to understanding how to improve a system's
performance by comparing the best configuration to the current one.
Additionally, it enables the use of performance measures that are difficult to
minimize through gradient-based methods.
In this study, we developed a genetic algorithm to find the best system
configuration for a multi-agent system, specifically designed to manage
complex tasks.
We applied this method to a system called Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF),
which is a challenging problem that arises in various real-world scenarios.
We created a new evaluation framework to assess the performance of MAPF
solvers and discovered that optimization can significantly enhance their
performance.
We found that our solver, which uses genetic algorithms, is highly efficient
and can handle large-scale instances of the MAPF problem.
We also discovered that it is possible to achieve high performance using
simple heuristics and that the performance can be further improved by
fine-tuning the system configuration.

In this study, we examine the rate at which operators expand in size within a broad class of quantum systems that include holographic duals and chaotic dynamics. By utilizing symmetry properties, we establish that an operator's growth can be represented as the expansion of its associated shadow within a specific algebraic structure, namely the AdS geometry. This connection allows us to leverage symmetry principles to determine the growth of operators under time evolution, specifically those that correspond to fields with a defined spin. By applying this method, we derive the rate of growth for a wide range of operators, including single, composite, and highly entangled operators, and we find that the results are consistent with previous studies. Moreover, we establish that the relationship between operator growth and the expansion of their dual geometric representations is not merely coincidental, but rather a direct consequence of the underlying bulk dynamics. This connection allows us to derive the rate of operator growth directly from the equations of motion governing the fields in the bulk.

In indoor positioning systems, a common approach is to use a map-based technique that relies on estimating distances between geospatial locations based on WiFi signal strength. This paper proposes a machine learning method to enhance distance estimation accuracy, which in turn improves position estimation accuracy. A dataset was collected in a university building using various devices, and a dataset was created to train and test the model. The model was trained using a dataset of 10,000 samples and tested on a separate dataset of 10,000 locations. The results showed that the model achieved a 1.5-meter mean error in distance estimation, which was 1.2 meters better than a baseline model. This improvement in distance estimation accuracy led to a 1.2-meter reduction in mean position estimation error. The proposed model is lightweight and can be easily integrated into existing map-based positioning systems.

The concept of a Type II civilization, capable of utilizing a planet's entire energy output, is explored in this paper. We examine the energy sources available to a Type II civilization, including the energy from its host star, nuclear reactions, and the conversion of gravitational energy, to determine which source is capable of providing the largest possible energy output. We also consider the energy output of a Type II civilization in relation to its host star's characteristics and the planet's properties. Our analysis reveals that a Type II civilization could potentially achieve an energy output of up to 10^27 Watts, which is comparable to the energy output of the Sun. We also discuss the implications of this energy output on the detectability of such civilizations using current and future telescopes.

This paper proposes a novel approach to network performance monitoring using a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) architecture. By leveraging the benefits of a distributed system, we develop a content delivery network that can detect Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations and monitor performance by analyzing the P2P traffic. Our approach enables the detection of SLA breaches and the analysis of network performance, including latency and packet loss, by examining the timing and flow of data within the network. Our proposed solution is validated through a proof-of-concept implementation and numerical analysis.

A study was conducted to analyze the effect of different filling patterns on threshold current and beam loading in a specific ERLinac design. The study found that certain filling patterns can lead to increased threshold current and beam loading, and that the beam loading effect can be mitigated by choosing a filling pattern that minimizes the overlap of the beams in the cavity. The total neutron cross section in a scintillator was measured between 98 and 688 MeV using the NA61/09 experiment at CERN's SPS. The setup included a forward hadron spectrometer and a 1.5 m thick scintillator target, with a backward neutron detector. The cross section was determined by comparing the number of incident and transmitted neutrons, and it was found to be approximately 150 cm^2 for neutrons with a mean free path of around 10 cm.

The process of planet formation is initiated by the accumulation of solid particles in a protoplanetary disk, with the transition from small particles to larger bodies known as planetesimals being a critical step. This step is still not fully understood, and our research aims to shed light on it by examining the sticking forces between particles in the temperature range of 100-1000 K. We found that sticking forces increase significantly in this temperature range, with a notable rise from 600 K to 800 K, suggesting that planetesimal formation may be most likely to occur at temperatures above 600 K. This finding is consistent with the thermal conditions found in the warm region of a protoplanetary disk. We also found that the presence of water vapor in the gas phase does not affect the sticking forces between particles, which is an important consideration for the formation of icy planetesimals in the cooler regions of a protoplanetary disk. Our research provides a crucial step towards understanding the conditions required for the formation of planetary systems.

Local Fisher discriminant analysis (LFDA) is a supervised dimensionality reduction technique that localizes the data and identifies directions for optimal class separation in local neighborhoods. The R package 'kernlab' already includes functions for performing and visualizing LFDA and its supervised variant LSFA. However, these functions are based on a distance metric and are not applicable to data types such as binary data, compositional data, or data with a non-Euclidean structure. This paper introduces the local Fisher discriminant analysis using the geodesic distance (GLFDA) and its supervised counterpart (GLSFDA). The 'kernlab' package has been extended to incorporate these new methods, which are now available for visualization through the existing functions 'lfda' and 'lslda'.

Robotic skill learning through imitating demonstrations is often hindered by complex nonlinear constraints. To overcome this challenge, we propose a constrained imitation learning approach that addresses the problem of learning skills with nonlinear hard constraints from demonstrated trajectories. By formulating the problem as an optimal control problem with inequality constraints, we develop an efficient solution using a loss function that penalizes deviations from demonstrated trajectories and hard constraints. To ensure real-time applicability, we utilize a sparse grid collocation method to parameterize the control input and solve the problem. Our approach is validated on a mobile robot, where we demonstrate its ability to learn skills that satisfy multiple nonlinear hard constraints from demonstrated trajectories.

We establish a direct link between the two-gluon color evanescent waveform in QCD and specific six-gluon amplitudes within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. This connection is achieved by constructing a particular six-gluon amplitude that utilizes the evanescent gluons as external legs. This constructed amplitude is then shown to be directly related to the desired two-gluon CEV. As a result, we derive a novel, compact formula for the leading-logarithmic two-gluon CEV in QCD. This formula is derived from the sum of $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills amplitudes that are conformally equivalent to the six specific gluons involved. This connection between the amplitude and the CEV provides a novel, geometric understanding of the two-gluon Casimir expansion.

We investigate a model of spin-orbit coupled electrons on a honeycomb lattice, coupled to an $s$-wave attractive bosonic boson, to understand the interplay between superconductivity and topology. Our analysis reveals that the gap in the electronic spectrum can be maintained even after the opening of a superconducting gap, indicating a topological phase. The model exhibits robust edge modes resistant to backscattering from defects, and the application of a magnetic field can induce a transition from a topological phase to a Chern insulator.

Our research reveals a lattice symmetry breaking transition in the vortex lattice of $d$-wave superconductors near a van Hove singularity, in line with theoretical predictions. This transition, from a square to a diagonal vortex lattice, is consistent with the predictions made by the Ginzburg-Landau theory and the BCS theory. Our findings are supported by experimental evidence from scanning tunneling microscopy and muon spin resonance, which show the same lattice symmetry change in $d$-wave superconducting materials.

We investigated the free energy of stretching polymers in a brush on a curved surface, in comparison to one on a flat surface. The self-avoiding walk model was used to analyze this, and the brush was assumed to be in a fully stretched state. The general curvature of the substrate was taken into account, while the curvature along the polymer chains was neglected. The energy of stretching was calculated for both brush configurations, and the results showed that the curvature of the surface has a significant impact on the brush's extension, with the effect being proportional to the square of the brush's height and the general curvature of the substrate. The brush's extension is increased when the substrate is positively curved, and decreased when it is negatively curved. The results also indicate that the brush's extension is not affected by the density of the polymer chains, and the comparison between the results and previous studies revealed that the brush's extension is increased when the polymer chains are densely packed.

The graph metric dimension was initially defined and its properties were explored. A new definition of graph distance was then introduced, specifically the truncated distance, and its impact on the metric dimension was analyzed. It was found that for a given graph, the truncated distance dimension remains equal to the metric dimension for short distances, but changes significantly once the distance threshold is exceeded. A formula was also derived to calculate the dimension for a graph with a specific distance structure.

Understanding the long-term variability of active galactic nuclei is crucial, yet it's complicated by the need for extensive, multi-year observations. Analyzing such data is further hindered by the presence of multiple timescales of variability and the varying data coverage over time. To address this challenge, we developed a novel statistical model that accounts for the non-uniform sampling and the multiple variability timescales. This model, a Bayesian hierarchical Gaussian process, allows for the estimation of the underlying variability pattern and its associated uncertainties. We applied this model to the analysis of the optical variability of Mrk 590, using data from the Catalina Real-Time Transient Survey spanning 10 years. The results show that the Gaussian process model can accurately capture the variability pattern and that the model's hyperparameters are consistent with the physical properties of the AGN. The model's ability to handle the varying data coverage and estimate the variability pattern and its uncertainties makes it a valuable tool for the analysis of long-term observations of active galactic nuclei.

In various contexts, such as allocating resources to individuals, valuations are often based on relationships between items, which can be represented as graphs. This study investigates the impact of graph structures on the difficulty of approximating social welfare, specifically focusing on valuations based on bipartite graphs, star graphs, and directed graphs. It demonstrates that even in these scenarios, there is no constant-factor approximation algorithm for social welfare unless P equals NP, and the difficulty increases with the size of the graph. However, it also shows that for bipartite graphs, a factor of $n^{\epsilon}$ approximation is achievable for any $\epsilon > 0$, and for directed graphs, an $O(\log n)$ approximation is possible.

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of point spread functions in the Pan-STARRS1 survey data, which is crucial for identifying binary asteroids in wide-field surveys. We examine the factors that influence the PSF shape, including the presence of a secondary component, and develop a method to quantify the ellipticity of the PSF. We also explore the relationship between the separation of binary asteroids and the detectability of the secondary component, and establish a criterion for identifying binary candidates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a case study of the binary asteroid 2004 FH, and show that our approach can be used to identify binary asteroids in wide-field surveys.

This paper introduces a new approach to analyzing peer effects in networks, which can be applied to a wide range of economic research topics. We propose a method that uses instrumental variables in conjunction with network data to create a reliable estimation technique based on GMM. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we utilize a large dataset from the Current Population Survey to examine the impact of social networks on individuals' labor force participation. Our findings reveal that network influences have a significant impact on labor force participation, with an increase of 10 percentage points in the network's rate of non-participation leading to a 1 percentage point rise in an individual's likelihood of being employed.

This paper introduces multiple chain rule formulas for variable-order fractional operators, including the Riemann-Liouville and Caputo types, in addition to a general form. The proofs utilize the relationship between these operators and their respective integral forms. The variable order Riemann-Liouville and Caputo operators chain rule formulas are derived from their respective integral forms. The chain rule formulas proposed in this study are also applied to establish the chain rule for the variable order Caputo adjoint operator.

In complex multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, a research study proposes a novel optimal Bayesian detector for distinguishing between two possible transmitted signals. The problem is made more challenging by the presence of unknown parameters and a non-Gaussian distribution of a random variable. The optimal solution, however, proves computationally infeasible. A new approach is then presented, which provides the best performance among all detectors that rely on linear statistics. This proposed detector is found to have an error rate that is significantly lower than other commonly used methods, and in some cases, the difference is as much as 1 dB. The study also reveals that the performance of this proposed detector is comparable to the optimal Bayesian detector, with the difference being less than 0.5 dB in most scenarios. The study's results are supported by numerical simulations.

developed to analyze the BASS survey data. This tool is versatile and can be
applied to any spectral dataset. By doing so, it enables us to extract
statistically significant information from the data. We have demonstrated the
effectiveness of BASS in analyzing the BASS survey data, but it can also be
used to analyze other galaxy surveys. The BASS code can be easily adapted to
accommodate different types of surveys, and it can also be used to analyze
spectra from different instruments. The BASS code is written in Python and is
available on GitHub.

The breakup of Gondwana led to the formation of various continental margins, which can be categorized into passive and active types. This study investigates the relationship between the direction and velocity of extension during breakup and the resulting marginal structures. By analyzing the distribution of passive and active margins, we found that the majority of these margins were formed in areas of slow extension, while areas of fast extension were characterized by complex active margins. Furthermore, we discovered that the type of marginal structure is not solely determined by the velocity of extension, but also by the direction of extension. This study also found that the majority of the Earth's surface is composed of passive margins, which are more likely to form in areas of fast extension. This study provides a framework for understanding the relationship between the distribution of passive and active margins and the distribution of slow and fast extension zones.

We introduce a new unsupervised pre-training framework for segmentation that leverages only image content, making it applicable to a wide range of datasets. Our framework is built on two key principles: ensuring semantic consistency across different image representations and enforcing the independence of image content from segmentation masks. To achieve these principles, we employ a contrastive learning approach to align the image features and a mask-aware attention mechanism to decouple the image content and segmentation masks. Our method outperforms existing unsupervised pre-training techniques in a fine-tuning evaluation, and our analysis shows that our approach effectively learns semantically meaningful image representations.

Human collaboration is a fundamental aspect of our social interactions, and it is a critical component of our ability to thrive as a society. Collaborative activities, such as group projects, require individuals to work together towards a common goal, and they are essential for the successful completion of complex tasks. In this context, we are interested in exploring how individuals can work together to achieve a common goal in a complex and dynamic environment, such as a game. To this end, we have developed a novel approach that combines elements of a theory-of-mind with a goal-oriented framework, and we have evaluated our approach through a series of collaborative games. Our results demonstrate that our approach is effective in facilitating successful goal achievement in collaborative settings, and we believe that our work has important implications for the development of collaborative systems and the advancement of artificial intelligence.

Linguistic evolution is a natural occurrence, with new words emerging and existing ones shifting in meaning over time. Identifying such changes in meaning is a challenging task for researchers, as it requires a deep understanding of language and its complexities. In this research, we propose a novel approach to this problem by leveraging pre-trained language models and fine-tuning them on large corpora. By analyzing the semantic representations of words in these models, we can identify words that have undergone significant meaning changes. Our experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately detecting such changes. Additionally, we explore the impact of different training strategies on the results and provide a comprehensive analysis of our findings.

We introduce two novel concepts, the parton transverse momentum distribution and the parton intrinsic conditional probability distribution, to address the motion of partons in a direction perpendicular to the parton's momentum.

This study investigates the topological constraints imposed by knots on the folding pathways of proteins, with a focus on the relationship between knot depth and folding speed. To explore this, we simulated the folding of shallow and deeply knotted proteins, as well as a series of proteins with varying levels of knot depth, using a lattice model. Our results demonstrate that shallow and deeply knotted proteins exhibit distinct folding pathways, with shallow knots leading to a slower folding speed compared to deeply knotted proteins. Additionally, we found that the folding speed of proteins is directly related to the depth of their knots, with a more deeply knotted protein leading to a faster folding speed. Our findings also reveal that the folding pathway of shallow knots involves a prolonged wandering phase, during which the knot slowly traverses the protein chain, whereas deeply knotted proteins fold quickly, with the knot becoming trapped in a small loop. These results provide valuable insights into the relationship between topological constraints and protein folding dynamics.

In this study, we investigate the impact of Early Dark Energy (EDE) on the Hubble Tension, a discrepancy in the measurement of the universe's expansion rate. We utilize a comprehensive statistical analysis to compare the predictions of a specific EDE model to observational data from the Cosmic Microwave Background and large-scale structure, as well as local measurements of the expansion rate. We find that the EDE model allows for a range of parameters that alleviate the Hubble Tension, with the allowed range depending on the parameters of the cosmological model. We also find that the EDE model is consistent with the size of the universe's fluctuations observed in the early universe, as well as the expansion rate measured in the local universe. Our results suggest that the EDE model is a viable alternative to the standard cosmological model, and that further research is needed to determine the nature of the EDE field.

Given a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ that does not have any non-trivial de Rham cohomology, we establish a condition for $\omega$ that is necessary and sufficient. This condition can be modified to include the property that the $k$-th Betti number of $M$ is greater than zero, where $k$ is any integer greater than or equal to one.

We propose a new model for mass generation, where a massive Nambu-Goldstone boson emerges from a spontaneous symmetry breaking process. This model is based on the idea of kaon condensation and can be described using an effective Lagrangian. By applying the linear sigma model, we calculate the masses of the condensate fields and determine the masses of scalar and pseudoscalar kaon states. These calculations show that the mass of the condensate states is equal to the mass of the NGB condensate, which is a unique feature of this model. This model can be applied to kaon condensation in nuclear matter and may provide a new understanding of the kaon condensation phenomenon.

We propose a training method called DISCO, which generates counterfactual data to enhance the robustness of machine learning models. By creating diverse perturbations, DISCO produces a range of counterfactual data that can be used to train models. We found that models trained with this method are more resistant to adversarial attacks and generalize better, particularly when trained with a larger number of counterfactual samples.

For a circulant graph $G = Z_n(2,3)$ with $n$ being an odd integer greater than 6, this study finds that both its neighborhood sum distinguishing total chromatic number and equitable sum distinguishing total chromatic number equal 3.

Researchers have developed a novel technique for synthesizing high-quality epitaxial domains of GaAs on graphene using molecular beam epitaxy. The process involves the self-assembly of atomic layers of GaAs, resulting in the formation of different types of domains with distinct crystal orientations. The size and distribution of these domains can be controlled by adjusting the growth temperature. The highest quality domains exhibit a similar structure to the underlying graphene substrate, while the lowest quality domains have a different crystal structure. The researchers also found that the quality of the GaAs layers is significantly affected by the presence of a buffer layer of GaAs, which can be used to improve the overall quality of the GaAs layers. The research has important implications for the development of advanced electronic devices based on graphene and other 2D materials.

This study presents the construction of several rank-bounded $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes using the method of taking the direct sum of codes defined on different bases, and examines the impact of this method on rank in detail. It also analyzes the rank of several specific $\mathbb{Z}_3 \mathbb{Z}_9$-linear codes and highlights the significance of rank determination in code design. It further discusses the relationship between rank and idempotents, and the connection between generator matrices and idempotents.

This research examines the interaction between two polymer streams with different viscosities, which are combined at a 90-degree angle before being pushed into a channel. The viscosities of the polymers are not constant and are instead influenced by the rate at which they are being pushed, which is taken into account using the Phan-Thien-Tanner model. The rate at which the polymer streams meet is not uniform and is instead affected by the viscosities of the polymers, which is demonstrated through numerical simulations. The results of these simulations are then compared to the outcomes of previous experiments and the findings of other researchers. This paper introduces S2M, a novel data augmentation method that transforms single-to-multi-label images. Unlike previous approaches that randomly convert images or use complex models to generate new labels, S2M strategically converts images by leveraging existing data and existing annotation costs. It allows for the creation of multi-label data from single-label datasets, which is a common and cost-effective way to collect such data. The proposed method is evaluated on the Amazon-Prime dataset, and the results show that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This study investigates the initial value problem of a time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, specifically focusing on the existence of global weak solutions and their energy properties. We establish that solutions exist for the entire duration when using the Riemann-Liouville interpretation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's energy remains bounded over time, and in certain conditions, solutions converge to equilibrium states as time approaches infinity. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the Riemann-Liouville and Caputo interpretations, and prove that they yield equivalent results under specific constraints.

Weak naturality, a fundamental property in category theory, involves the interaction between functors and natural transformations. This paper introduces a novel concept, the weak universal property of weak adjunctions, which extends the universal property of categories to incorporate two 2-cells that represent the unit and counit of the adjunction. This new concept is then employed to characterize weak adjunctions in terms of the 2-functoriality of the category of endofunctors on a given category.

We investigate the electron heating rate's impact on the minimum action diffusion model's (MAD) ability to replicate GeV gamma-ray data, utilizing a simple analytical approach.  Our findings suggest that a higher electron heating rate diminishes the MAD model's effectiveness in accounting for this data.  Nevertheless, the model remains viable under a lower electron heating rate scenario.  Our research also reveals that the gamma-ray production rate is significantly influenced by the electron heating rate, with a notable decrease observed when the rate is increased.  As a result, the MAD model's predictions for the gamma-ray production rate are only consistent with observations when the electron heating rate is below a certain threshold, which is approximately 10^-10 times the rate of the cosmic ray energy dissipation.

This paper investigates the statistical properties of a portfolio constructed from the assets in the S&P 500, focusing on the distribution of daily returns. We analyze the portfolio's performance over a 20-year period, specifically from January 2nd, 2001 to December 31st, 2020, and our results demonstrate that the mean, standard deviation, and skewness of the portfolio's returns are consistent with the sum of the individual asset returns. Additionally, we find that the kurtosis of the portfolio's returns is approximately equal to the kurtosis of an individual asset's returns, and we provide a proof for this phenomenon. We also explore the implications of this result on the portfolio's probability of extreme events.

This research paper introduces a novel approach to detecting cardiac abnormalities using noisy electrocardiogram signals. A new method is presented that employs a Generative Adversarial Network to clean up noisy ECG data and then uses a Convolutional Neural Network to classify cardiac conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accurately identifying cardiac abnormalities, outperforming other methods in terms of accuracy, especially when dealing with noisy data.

The rise of activity tracking devices has led to a significant increase in data collected from users, which poses challenges in terms of storage, processing, and quality control. To address these issues, we propose FedHealth, a novel framework that leverages Federated Learning to enhance the accuracy of activity recognition while minimizing the need for data storage and processing. FedHealth utilizes a central server to coordinate the training of a shared model by multiple clients, who contribute to the training using their local data. The framework is designed to be robust to data inconsistencies and outliers, and it allows for the continuous improvement of the activity recognition model without the need for data transfer. Experimental results demonstrate that FedHealth outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and it has the potential to revolutionize the way activity tracking devices collect and process data.

This research focuses on enhancing portfolio management through optimization techniques. We examine the performance of various optimization methods, including single and multi-objective approaches, as well as linear and non-linear strategies. We also assess the effectiveness of using machine learning to improve portfolio performance. Our findings indicate that utility-based optimization yields the best results, while multi-objective optimization and linear approaches do not significantly outperform a buy-and-hold strategy. However, incorporating machine learning into linear models can enhance performance, albeit with limited statistical significance.

We propose a new model for dark energy, consisting of a quintessence field that is not coupled to itself and interacts with heavier states, such as a scalar field responsible for inflation and a dark matter component. This model allows for a unified understanding of both dark matter and dark energy, and we explore its implications for cosmic evolution, including the transition from an inflationary phase to a dark energy phase driven by the decay of the heavy states. We develop a general framework for analyzing the dynamics of this model, and we apply it to specific cases, such as a quintessence field with an exponential or inverse power law potential. We also investigate the possibility of a phase transition between the dark matter and dark energy phases, and we find that this transition can be triggered by the quintessence field reaching a critical value, at which point it begins to dominate the cosmic energy budget. Our results show that this model can be consistent with current observations, and we discuss the prospects for testing it through future experiments.

The surge in online job applications has made it increasingly difficult for companies to efficiently review candidates, particularly when scheduling interviews. To address this challenge, we propose using data-driven methods to streamline the interview process. By leveraging search techniques and optimization models, we aim to improve the efficiency of scheduling and creating recruitment panels. A real-world case study from a major Italian bank demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in scheduling interviews and forming panels with specific criteria.

This study explores the impact of a diffusion process on a given drift in relation to a backward stochastic differential equation with a singular terminal condition, specifically examining how this influence relates to the first eigenvalue of the underlying operator and the corresponding eigenfunction, and also discusses the behavior when this eigenvalue is not present among the operator's spectrum.

We investigate the asymmetric production of leptoquark pairs via a Drell-Yan process, requiring the presence of both initial state protons and antiprotons in a future $pp$ collider. This production mechanism allows for the creation of a leptoquark and an anti-leptoquark from the annihilation of a quark and an anti-quark. We establish constraints on the mass and coupling of the leptoquark based on current LHC data and explore the leptoquark's potential to explain anomalies in $B$-meson decays. We also assess the leptoquark's detectability at a 50 TeV $pp$ collider with 15 ab$^{-1}$ of data, considering both direct searches and flavor anomalies.

In time-dependent gene expression data analysis, identifying the predictive variables for a target variable is crucial. We've developed a new approach that combines relevance learning and time-series classification to efficiently pinpoint these predictive variables. Our method, ReLearn, initially uses relevance learning to filter out non-informative genes, and then employs a classification algorithm to identify the target variable using the remaining genes. We've demonstrated through experiments on synthetic data and real-world cancer gene expression datasets that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy and the number of selected features.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of 14 extreme starburst galaxies, focusing on their neutral carbon (CI) emissions at 155 $\mu$m, by obtaining new and/or previously unused data from various sources. We found that the CI line widths in these galaxies are significantly broader than expected, indicating the presence of low-density molecular outflows that are broader in scale than the line-emitting regions. We also discovered that the outflows in these galaxies are likely to be more widespread, and that the observed CI emissions may be influenced by the motion of molecular gas. We found that the ratios of [CI] to [CII] line emissions are not uniform across these galaxies, and that the ratios are affected by the presence of molecular outflows and the distribution of gas in the circumgalactic environment. We also discovered that the ratios of [CI] to far-infrared line emissions are not uniform, and that the ratios are affected by the presence of molecular outflows and the distribution of gas in the circumgalactic environment.
